Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/Reuters View image in fullscreen Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez has emerged as a leading left-wing European voice on the global stage, and endures having implemented a raft of progressive policies. Photograph: Yiannis Kourtoglou/Reuters First Edition newsletter Pedro Sánchez Monday briefing: What can Andy Burnham learn from Spain’s Pedro Sánchez? In today’s newsletter: The Spanish prime minister has remade himself as Europe’s leading leftwing standard-bearer. Could his success offer the UK’s PM a route forward? Michael Segalov Mon 17 Aug 2026 01.47 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 02.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. To international onlookers, Pedro Sánchez appears to have achieved the impossible. Where other European leftist and left-ish premiers have flopped and flailed, the Spanish PM has endured. Since June 2018, Sánchez has ruled from Madrid, implementing a raft of progressive policies. More recently, he has emerged as a leading, and often lone, left-wing European voice on the global stage, striking a defiant tone on everything from the Trump administration’s war in Iran (“the smokescreen of war to hide their failure”) to Israel’s actions in Gaza (“exterminating a defenceless people”). The fact that the international press has nicknamed him El Guapo (the handsome one) can’t hurt. At home, however, it’s a more complex story. Sánchez’s inner circle is in the midst of a damaging corruption scandal , and polling has his traditionally centre-left Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) faltering. Meanwhile, recent scenes in Ceuta and apocalyptic wildfires throw up thorny policy challenges. European leaders have publicly turned on Sánchez – and this is with a general election looming next year. But just like the UK’s own prime minister, while Sánchez has carved out a name for himself, he was not always the left-wing figure he is seen as today. For today’s First Edition, we ask: who is the real Pedro Sánchez? And, what lessons can Andy Burnham learn from his tenure? Madrid-based journalist Eoghan Gilmartin helps us answer these questions. Before that, the headlines: Weekend roundup UK economy | The UK should expect to see a new cost of living crisis , with official figures released this week by the ONS expected to show how soaring energy bills drove up inflation close to 3% in July. Ceuta | Moroccan police arrested 111 people this weekend, who were trying to enter Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, amid tightened security on both sides after social media posts called for another mass crossing. Jason Arday | The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday. UK politics | Andy Burnham is being urged to protect 4 million gig economy workers, who thinktanks warn miss out on key statutory rights including: parental leave, redundancy pay and protection against unfair dismissal. Indonesia | Rescue crews dug through collapsed buildings and landslide debris in eastern Indonesia on Sunday, searching for bodies after a powerful earthquake killed at least 51 people, and injured more than 100. In depth: The art of political reinvention View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham, the prime minister and former mayor of Greater Manchester, transformed his political fortunes when he left Westminster. Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP Andy Burnham and Pedro Sánchez share similar origin stories. Both initially entered, then departed, their respective parliaments having failed to achieve their ambitions; both returned, and subsequently secured the top job, after quiet reinvention. We know the Burnham story now: the former Blairite minister lost out on the Labour leadership, and instead became mayor of one of the UK’s largest cities, where he emerged transformed thanks to his vaguely articulated philosophy – Manchesterism. Sánchez too wasn’t always the progressive figurehead he is today. The former economics professor was first elected PSOE leader in 2014, firmly a centrist. “He was the compromise candidate between left and right,” says Gilmartin. “There were few expectations of him at the beginning.” His first stint at the party’s helm ended in 2016, after a series of electoral drubbings and a messy internal revolt saw him forced out by party grandees. And so marked the start of his remaking: 6ft 3in Sánchez squeezed into his Peugeot and road-tripped across España. “I’ll get in my car and travel all round Spain to listen to those who haven’t been listened to, to the grassroots members and left-wing voters,” Sánchez said. Sánchez understands that anchoring his party to the left … is where he can govern. Beyond Madrid, he morphed into an anti-establishment, man-of-the-people figure. By the summer of 2017, he was PSOE leader again. He formed a government in June 2018, and has been PM since. “He’s not necessarily a committed left-winger,” says Gilmartin, “but Sánchez understands that anchoring his party to the left and positioning himself as the leader of a wider progressive bloc is where he can govern. He’s a very impressive pragmatist.” In 2019, to shore up support from the left, Sánchez pledged to implement hundreds of progressive policies . And he has broadly delivered on this agenda: investing heavily in renewables, hiking up the minimum wage, extending abortion rights, banning so-called “gay conversion practices”, capping rent increases and raising taxes on the super-wealthy while reducing the tax burden on lower earners. Home and away That’s not to say Sánchez’s leadership has been smooth sailing. A series of corruption scandals involving his brother, wife and predecessor have emerged, many of which the PM had dismissed as “politically motivated smears.” Other confidantes have also been accused of taking kickbacks . Meanwhile, his minority coalition government can’t muster much support; they’ve not managed to pass a new budget since 2023. PSOE has lost a string of recent local elections. Ever the pragmatist, Sánchez shifted focus to the international. In the last year or so, Sánchez really took on Trump . He refused to approve the US military use of jointly operated bases to strike Iran, stating: “You cannot answer one illegality with another, because that is how the great catastrophes of humanity begin”. Spain formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024, with Sánchez labelling Israel’s actions in Gaza a “genocide” , and described Europe’s broader response as a “ failure ”. “His foreign policy has taken on a much more important role, showing that [he leads] a government with life,” says Gilmartin. Despite being a social democrat, he has embraced his reputation as the voice and conscious of the international left, hosting, in April, a star-studded left-wing jamboree in Barcelona to reinvigorate international progressive politics. All of this has helped coalesce support at home, though it hasn’t yet bolstered his domestic popularity significantly. A winning formula Eight years in, it’s no great surprise Sánchez’s popularity is on the wane. But his 2023 electoral success is worth considering. In the run up to that vote, he was on the brink of defeat. The right-wing People’s Party led the polls, with far-right Vox primed to come in third. It seemed a right/far-right coalition beckoned. But says Gilmartin, “by framing the vote as him against the far-right,” Sánchez was able to turn the tide, pointing out all the policy gains and social protections that would be under threat otherwise. Starmer tried this, too, in his 2025 Labour conference speech. But his vision of “patriotic national renewal under the Labour party … or the toxic divide and division of Reform” didn’t land. Starmer couldn’t communicate a coherent vision. He failed to point to policies that voters would miss. “Polarising against the right works for the centre left if you deliver on cost of living and other material issues,” says Gilmartin. Else, you’re left with the empty progressivism of say, Hillary Clinton taking on Trump. “That’s been proven to not be enough.” So, what are the lessons for Burnham? Burnham knows he has to deliver, with less than three years before the next general election. It looked initially that he might be bold on policy: announcing his intent to end homelessness on day one. But since then, (and in fairness, Burnham did take the reins right before a summer recess), he has gone rather quiet. And on both immigration and the environment – two major wedges between progressives and much of the right – he has said almost nothing at all. Sánchez took a different tack. One of his first acts as PM was allowing the Aquarius to dock in Valencia: the ship carrying 629 people rescued off the coast of Libya that had been turned away from Italy and Malta. Since then, Sánchez has moved to regularise undocumented migrants in Spain. After 72,000 mostly Moroccans crossed into Ceuta last month, Sánchez didn’t pander to the right, or bow to pan-European pressure. The results are clear: despite recent increases, Spanish people remain relatively unconcerned about immigration. In January, only 3.9% of Spaniards felt immigration was the biggest issue facing Spain; in June , it was 4.8%. Similarly on climate, Sánchez hasn’t held back. Where Burnham banned BBQs, Sánchez declared “ climate change kills ”. He’s spending billions on the green transition while Burnham dithers on north sea drilling . “There’s no sense here that you apologise for being proactive and progressive on climate,” says Gilmartin. In occupying this space, Sánchez has gobbled up the left-wing vote. Sumar, Sánchez’s left-of-PSOE coalition partners has dropped in the polls. When Sánchez first became PSO leader, further-to-the-left Podemos was polled up to 26%; today, it’s hovering at 3%. Burnham might do well to learn from this: because while Starmer made attacking the left a defining feature of his time in office, Labour lost almost four times as many voters to the Greens than to Reform in the 2026 local elections. For now, the wait continues to see if Burnham will prove a progressive PM, or at least an impressive pragmatist. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The week to come Monday | Nominations close for candidates seeking to replace Anas Sarwar as Scottish Labour leader. Tuesday | Opening arguments expected to begin in a lawsuit brought by multiple US states against Meta about social media addiction. Thursday | Students in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland will receive their GCSE results. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian Anna Moore’s deep dive on why women are expected to have hysterocopies without pain relief is brutal and important. Poppy Noor, deputy newsletters editor I’ve spent this heatwave-y summer feeling like a toddler sweating in sticky T-shirts and shorts. These insights from fashionistas about how and why they dress made me excited to wear grown up clothes again, weather-depending. Michael Emine Saner’s interview with Su Pollard is a must-read this morning. I particularly enjoyed all the funny stories of famous people she’s met. Poppy Sport View image in fullscreen Amy Hunt celebrates after victory at Alexander Stadium. Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty Images European Athletics Championships | Amy Hunt became the first to win four titles at a single event , while Dina Asher-Smith hit a record 11 European medals total. Football | Mikel Arteta said his Arsenal players demonstrated their hunger to defend the Premier League title in their Community Shield triumph over Manchester City. Cricket | Manchester Super Giants triumphed in the final of the men’s Hundred, surviving a late wobble to beat Trent Rockets by five wickets. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Boost special needs internships to tackle youth jobs crisis – Milburn”, is the Guardian ’s front page. The Times has “Disability claimants would swap cash for help”, the i Paper says “Thousands of new homes set to be built as Rayner tears up rules on green belt” and the FT writes “Dimon warns Healey not to raise bank taxes or risk driving finance jobs away”. Elsewhere, the Telegraph ’s splash is “Russia’s secret bases threaten Nato”, the Mail leads on “Paedophile fireman used loophole to keep changing his identity”, and the Express has “‘We’re entering a golden era for dementia research’”. The Mirror says “‘Murder by dog’”, and the Sun’ s splash is “Call this justice?”. Lastly, Metro , on water bills writes “Water cheek!”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Isolated on a hospital ward and not allowed any visitors except his wife, he began making music as a way to pass the time. Photograph: Manuel Vazquez/The Guardian The super-producer who made an album from his hospital bed James Ellis Ford been described as the music industry’s secret weapon; a producer loved by artists such as Arctic Monkeys, Pulp and Jessie Ware. In 2024, he was diagnosed with leukaemia and it all ground to a halt. With contributions from Jarvis Cocker and Jessie Ware , Nosheen Iqbal hears how making music f rom his hospital bed helped Ford through one of the hardest periods of his life. Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nicola Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen ‘We’re bringing the Dome back, baby,” said Tom Rothman, the CEO of Sony Pictures. Photograph: Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times/Getty The celebrated Cinerama dome is set to reopen in 2028 after five years closed, reports Matthew Cantor , in a hopeful sign for LA’s cinema culture. The historic 1963 theatre became a symbol of the struggles facing moviegoing after the Covid pandemic, prompting a grassroots campaign to save it. Its reopening comes amid a broader resurgence at the box office, driven by younger audiences, social media and a renewed appetite for communal experiences. Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images View image in fullscreen Homes in Pinole, California, on 3 September 2026. Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images US news US home sales slowest in more than a year as mortgage rates and prices climb Housing market has been stymied by borrowing costs, as Iran war pushed mortgage rates higher Associated Press Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.27 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 14.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Sales of previously occupied US homes declined in August to their slowest annual pace in more than a year as home shoppers grappled with rising mortgage rates and home prices. Existing home sales fell 2% last month from July to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98m units, the National Association of Realtors said on Thursday. This is the third straight monthly decline. Sales also fell 1.2% compared with August last year. The latest sales tally is just shy of the 4m pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet. “It’s not a surprise home sales and mortgage rates move in the opposite direction and we have seen mortgage rates rising, rising, rising from February,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist. Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4m annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2m. The last time the annual sales pace came in below 4m was June 2025. Despite the latest pullback, existing US home sales are running 1.6% higher through the first eight months of this year than they were in the same stretch of 2025, NAR said. The housing market has been stymied in large part by rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have marched higher in the months since the war between the US and Iran started in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher. The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage hit 6.76% this week, its highest level in more than 14 months. It briefly dipped below 6% before the war started. Yun noted that rate could soon reach 7%, given that mortgage rates tend to follow moves in the 10-year treasury yield, which is at levels not seen since late 2023. The yield was at 4.92% on the bond market as of Thursday morning. Even as sales slowed, home prices continued to rise nationally last month. The US median sales price increased 1.6% in August from a year earlier to $429,100, an all-time high for the month of August based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis for 38 months in a row. The US housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied US homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. Years of soaring home prices, especially in the early part of this decade when rock-bottom mortgage rates fueled a buying frenzy, have left many would-be homebuyers frozen out of the market. And a chronic shortage of homes for sale nationally, due partly to years of below-average new home construction, has helped prop up home prices even in a multi-year sales slump. Many of the homes bought last month probably went under contract in July and June, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.43% to 6.66%. Regionally, sales fell last month from July in the north-east, midwest and south. Sales were flat in the west. Prices, meanwhile, continued to rise in the north-east faster than the rest of the country, climbing 4.3% from August last year amid a shortage of homes on the market relative to other regions. The sales slowdown is leading to unsold properties sitting on the market longer, helping boost the number of available homes. Although home inventory levels remain well below historical norms, there were 1.62m unsold homes at the end of last month, up 3.2% from July and up 5.9% from August last year, NAR said. That is still short of the roughly 2m homes for sale that was typical before the Covid-19 pandemic. Still, August’s month-end inventory translates to a 4.9-months’ supply at the current sales pace. That is the highest level in over 10 years. Traditionally, a four- to six-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers. The increase in homes for sale gives home shoppers who can afford to buy at current mortgage rates or pay all cash a wider selection and potentially more leverage in negotiating better sales terms. In August, the national median home listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier, while roughly 20% of listings had their initial price lowered, according to Realtor.com. First-time buyers accounted for 30% of home purchases last month, up from 29% in July and 28% in August last year, NAR said. Historically, first-time buyers make up closer to 40% of home sales. Affordability remains a primary concern for home shoppers, as home prices, mortgage rates, property taxes and insurance costs are now significantly higher than a few years ago, noted Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. The trends are also putting pressure on homeowners eager to sell. “It’s not a good time to sell your home,” Long said. “Americans are hitting the pause button on homebuying.” Explore more on these topics US news US house prices US mortgages US interest rates US personal finance Economics US economy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

https://www.politico.eu/article/french-p.text: PARIS — French presidential candidate Edouard Philippe pitched gradually raising the country’s legal age of retirement from 64 to 65 for most workers in his much-anticipated pensions reform plan unveiled on Tuesday. Philippe, a center-right former prime minister whose campaign has yet to gain traction against his populist rivals, said in a nearly 20-minute video that reforming the country’s generous pension system was imperative given France’s increasingly dire fiscal outlook. “We need to take the right decisions before the [financial] crisis that is set to hit us,” he said. “All European countries, whether governed by the right or the left, Germany, Spain... have implemented this. We are the only ones who haven’t.” Advertisement Advertisement The proposal also included gradually introducing some capitalization, in which a worker’s contributions are invested for their future retirement, into the system. He also wants to require people to make monthly contributions for 45 years instead of 43. Philippe’s plan appears largely in line with his pitch to voters as a fiscally responsible candidate who won’t hide from the truth. But retirement reform is one of French politics’ most explosive issues. French President Emmanuel Macron’s flagship reform in 2023, which raised the age to 64 for most workers, sparked massive protests and was so unpopular that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had to delay its implementation until after next year’s presidential election to save his government from being toppled. Philippe is struggling to hit his stride in a campaign currently dominated by far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, who proposed bringing the retirement age down to 62 at an estimated cost of €9 billion per year, and surging far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who wants the retirement age back at 60. Recent polls showed Mélenchon beating Philippe for second place and a spot in the runoff against Le Pen. Philippe tried to soften the blow, pledging that one in three French citizens would be able to retire early under his plan because their jobs are physically taxing. Advertisement Advertisement “It’s not a favor but the recognition of reality ... for the nurse who has been lifting patients for twenty years and who works nights at hospital ... for the truck driver who spent his life on the road,” he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/3.text: Listen (7 mins) Save Share Protests outside Poland’s constitutional court: What’s the crisis about? on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google A woman carrying a child stands in front of police officers in riot gear as protesters gather outside the headquarters of Poland's Constitutional Court in Warsaw after police blocked access to the building on October 31, 2026 [AFP] By Caolán Magee Published On 31 Oct 2026 31 Oct 2026 Riot police have been deployed outside Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal as a dispute over who should serve on the court escalates into a confrontation between Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government and the nationalist opposition. Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the Warsaw building on Friday night after judges elected by the current parliamentary majority announced the suspension of the tribunal’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski. Recommended Stories list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Flávio Bolsonaro vows to continue father’s political fight in Brazil list 2 of 4 Lebanon charges 13 over confiscated Hezbollah explosives list 3 of 4 Rival US and Russian resolutions on Western Sahara fail at UN list 4 of 4 Wounded Arsenal seek redemption in Anfield test against Liverpool end of list The move drew condemnation from the far-right opposition Law and Justice party, known as PiS, and prompted President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally, to abandon a trip to Senegal, turning his plane around to return to Poland on Friday. Police said three people were arrested after trying to enter the court complex. Tusk says decisive action is necessary to restore the rule of law after years of political interference in the Constitutional Tribunal under PiS. Here is what we know. Why are Poland’s leaders fighting over the Constitutional Tribunal? The Constitutional Tribunal decides whether laws comply with Poland’s constitution. Its rulings can prevent legislation from taking effect, making its independence and who sits on its bench politically significant. This latest dispute can be traced back to 2015, during the transfer of power from a centrist government led by Tusk’s Civic Platform party to the far-right PiS. The outgoing parliament elected five judges, although Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal subsequently found that only three of those appointments had a valid legal basis. The incoming PiS majority then elected replacements, including for the three seats already lawfully filled. Then-President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in the three validly elected judges. Advertisement During its eight years in government, PiS introduced broader judicial changes that critics said brought the courts under greater political influence. PiS is currently the main opposition in Poland. “It was a power play to control who serves as a justice, in what positions, and how the court system operates in Poland,” Wojciech Przybylski, editor-in-chief of Visegrad Insight, told Al Jazeera. “The former PiS government wanted a court system and tribunal that would allow it to pass laws that supported their ideological perspective. It also wanted control of a Constitutional Tribunal that would support its claim of sovereignty over the EU.” Aleksandra Kustra-Rogatka, an associate professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Torun, told Al Jazeera that “after Przylebska became president of the CC, the rule of law crisis worsened. Controversial laws reformed the judicial system, and the court became seen as a rubber-stamp body and an active political player supporting illiberal policies.” The European Court of Human Rights, which is separate from the EU, had already ruled in 2021 that an improperly appointed judge’s participation deprived a company of its right to a tribunal established by law. Then, in December 2025, the EU’s highest court ruled that the tribunal had not met the requirements of an independent court. It also found that tribunal judgements challenging the authority of EU law breached Poland’s obligations as a member state. Tusk returned to office as prime minister in December 2023 promising to restore judicial independence, and his government has refused to recognise the tribunal’s legitimacy in its existing form and has been attempting to disregard its rulings. Kustra-Rogatka added that “many supporters of the centrist governing camp have grown disappointed by the lack of progress in restoring the rule of law since 2023, partly constrained by the prospect of losing the 2025 presidential election”. This year, the parliament elected eight judges to the 15-member tribunal. President Nawrocki, a supporter of Donald Trump, was elected last year and with the power to veto legislation, administered the oath to three judges but withheld it from five, who instead took their oaths without his presence. The tribunal’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, refused to allow those five to begin adjudicating. What triggered the latest confrontation? On Friday, Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced one-month suspensions of court president Swieczkowski and his deputy, Sochanski, and said she was assuming responsibility for running the tribunal. Advertisement But questions have arisen over whether Korwin-Piotrowska, who is one of the court’s 15 justices alongside Swieczkowski and Sochanski, has the authority to do this. Her claim rests on her length of judicial service overall, rather than having served longest on the tribunal. In separate measures, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, took steps that could lead to criminal proceedings against the suspended president, Swieczkowski, and his deputy, Sochanski. Far-right critics say these measures are politically motivated and intended to apply pressure on the already suspended justices. PiS supporters, including senior party figures, gathered outside to oppose the suspensions on Friday. Police said their deployment followed information from Korwin-Piotrowska about possible threats to judges and staff and risks to public order. They said officers were securing the grounds and had not entered the tribunal building. Nawrocki turned back to Poland midair while flying to Senegal and arrived at the tribunal during the night. By Saturday morning, he had called urgent consultations with parliamentary representatives, describing events as a forcible takeover of a constitutional institution. Tusk defended the effort to restore the rule of law, saying that reversing the legacy of PiS required difficult action. What could happen next? The confrontation raises two overlapping questions: who is entitled to sit on the tribunal, and whether the measures used to change its leadership are lawful. Marcin Matczak, a prominent Polish lawyer, told Al Jazeera that the far-right opposition was defending its “remaining institutional stronghold”, while the centrist government wants to “restore balance to the Constitutional Tribunal”. But restoring independence also requires scrutiny of the current government’s choices. In September, its parliamentary majority elected Maciej Berek, previously a minister in Tusk’s cabinet, to the tribunal. Some coalition members opposed the appointment, saying it contradicted promises to depoliticise the judiciary. With parliamentary elections due next year, Matczak said Tusk might be taking a harder line to mobilise supporters frustrated by the slow pace of reform. “But that is a risky strategy: it may energise his political base while alienating more moderate voters,” he said. A more immediate flashpoint could be a tribunal judges’ meeting that Matczak said had been called for November 3. Attempts to lift immunity could deepen the confrontation if the assembly’s composition or ability to reach the required quorum is challenged. Matczak also warned that the scenes could establish a precedent for future governments. “A future government could invoke these events to argue that sending the police into the Constitutional Tribunal is an acceptable way to resolve a legal dispute,” he said. “Whatever the immediate political gains, the long-term institutional consequences could be deeply damaging.”
